name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,225

clue.text: Worker on vegetables? Could be

blocks.note: peas are a common green vegetable
the worker ant is the crossword's favourite worker

explanation.surface: A gardener toiling over the vegetable patch, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means 'placed after', so the worker follows the greens. The whole clue also describes a farm labourer, which 'Could be' admits.
explanation.definitionFit: A peasant is a poor farm labourer, someone who might well spend the day tending crops in a field.

clue.text: Info that’s spread on behalf of heathen father

blocks.note: pro is Latin for 'for', as in pro bono
a pagan is a heathen, one outside the main religions
da is an informal word for dad

explanation.surface: Gossip being put about concerning an unbelieving father.
explanation.walkthrough: Three plain pieces in clue order; the only trick is reading 'on behalf of' as the single short word PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is biased information deliberately circulated to sway public opinion, hence information that is spread.

clue.text: Rubbish about rising thespian

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising reads from the bottom upward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: rot is nonsense, rubbish
ca is the abbreviation of circa, about

explanation.surface: A complaint that an up-and-coming performer is talking nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is not a container signal here but the abbreviation CA; ROT + CA then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A thespian is a stage performer, named after Thespis, the legendary first actor of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Rule as yet misguidedly in a severe manner

indicators.note: something done misguidedly goes wrong, so the letters end up in a mistaken order

blocks.note: nine letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Governing harshly and wrongly, as a tyrant has done so far.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a harsh regime; the first three words are just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere means stern and strict, so acting austerely is behaving with harsh, unadorned strictness.

clue.text: Kept an eye on temperature — felt unwell

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for temperature
to ail is to be ill

explanation.surface: A nurse monitoring a fever in a patient who was poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is medical, so 'Kept an eye on' seems to go with temperature; it is the detective's sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to follow and watch them secretly, the way a detective shadows a suspect.

clue.text: Closed one large book

blocks.note: a door pushed to is shut
'one' can mean oneself, the speaker

explanation.surface: Someone shutting a heavy volume.
explanation.walkthrough: TO as an adverb means into the closed position, as in 'pull the door to'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tome is a big, heavy volume, especially a scholarly one.

clue.text: Money for waiting at table? Mine’s raised

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters lifts the last to the top, turning the order backwards

blocks.note: a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: A waiter asking about gratuities, then boasting that theirs has gone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive pronoun but is the noun for a colliery.
explanation.definitionFit: A gratuity is extra cash left by diners for the server who brought their food.

clue.text: Damage can with one cocktail

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
a tin is a can
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Spoiling a drink by mixing it with something from a can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' is the noun tin, not the verb, and 'with' just joins the cocktail to its recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A martini is a classic mixed drink of gin or vodka with vermouth.

clue.text: Like a bloom locust oddly destroyed

indicators.note: wiping out the odd-numbered positions leaves only every second letter standing

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A swarm of insects ravaging the flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' usually keeps the odd letters; 'destroyed' reverses that, so the even ones survive.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower that is out has opened fully, in bloom.

clue.text: Indoor footwear beginning to yield as it is on ice

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the adjective

indicators.note: a beginning is a start, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: a soft shoe worn about the house
first letter

explanation.surface: House shoes giving way underfoot on an icy path.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures slipping on ice in the wrong shoes; the definition is how things are on ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice is smooth and gives no grip, so walking on it is treacherous and hard to keep footing.

clue.text: Term pedant confused in specialised area

indicators.note: a confused thing is muddled, so its letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A fussy scholar muddled over jargon in his own field.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's pedant and his specialist field go together naturally, hiding that two words are just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A department is a division of an organisation or a sphere of knowledge handled by particular specialists.

clue.text: Share the view a deadly sin has no end

indicators.note: something with no end is cut short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
greed, or avarice, is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Agreeing that a deadly sin is never satisfied.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests greed is endless; the phrase actually tells you to lop the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To agree is to hold the same opinion as someone else, sharing their outlook.

clue.text: Reason for doing something on energy is sensitive

blocks.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
a motive is a reason behind an action

explanation.surface: Why someone acts on energy policy is a touchy subject.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, so the reason follows the energy.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotive issue arouses strong feelings, much like a sensitive subject that needs careful handling.

clue.text: Buy too much — lots of deliveries await settlement

blocks.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, so overs are batches of deliveries
a matter that pends is awaiting a decision

explanation.surface: A shopping spree: parcels arriving while the bills await payment.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'deliveries' parcels and 'settlement' paying bills; in fact deliveries are balls bowled in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: To overspend is to exceed a budget, purchasing more than one can afford.

clue.text: Strange rant about the French horn

indicators.note: something strange is out of the ordinary, so these letters lose their usual order
to be about something is to go around it, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
le is a French word for 'the'

explanation.surface: An odd tirade concerning a French horn, the brass instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French horn' reads as the instrument, but 'the French' is LE and 'horn' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An antler is the branched bony growth on a deer's head, loosely called a horn.

clue.text: Kills fish on ship’s upper deck

blocks.note: to top someone is slang for killing them
the ide is a freshwater fish, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A sailor catching and killing fish on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'A on B' sets A above B, so the killing sits over the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Topside is the part of a vessel above the waterline, and in naval usage means up on deck.

clue.text: Make changes to retain viewer’s backing?

indicators.note: making changes means altering, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A TV producer tweaking a show to keep its audience's support.
explanation.walkthrough: The viewer is an eye, not a TV watcher, and its backing is the lining at the back; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive layer lining the rear of the eyeball, the organ we see with.

clue.text: Wartime PM’s not bad for organised religion

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to go without something, removing it from the name

blocks.note: Winston Churchill was Britain's prime minister through most of the Second World War
ill means bad, as in ill effects

explanation.surface: Praising a wartime leader as a good friend of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not bad' sounds like faint praise, but it says to drop ILL from the statesman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A church is a Christian denomination or institution, a structured body of believers.

clue.text: Incline vocally to give approval to painting on two panels

indicators.note: done with the voice, so we go by how the words are spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: a dip is a downward slope
to tick something is to mark it as approved

explanation.surface: Leaning in to murmur praise of a two-part artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Said out loud, 'dip tick' matches the art term; the Greek spelling is the hurdle.
explanation.definitionFit: A diptych is an artwork, often an altarpiece, made of two hinged panels.

clue.text: Go quickly small bird

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a coot is a black water bird

explanation.surface: A little bird darting away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small bird' reads as one phrase, but it splits into S and the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoot is to dash off hurriedly, informally speaking.

clue.text: Top garden party?

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the verb, read whimsically as two words

blocks.note: first meaning: to beat or surpass
second meaning, split in two: an outdoor 'do', or party

explanation.surface: Praising the best garden party of the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective praising the party; it is a verb. A 'do' is informal British for a party, and one in the garden is an out-do.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo a rival is to surpass or beat them, which is what topping them means.

clue.text: Underclothes hang around airer regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so we keep every second letter

blocks.note: to linger is to loiter, stay on
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Underwear hung up to dry on a clothes horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hang around' fits the laundry scene literally; it is LINGER. An airer is a clothes-drying rack.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingerie is women's underwear and nightwear, typically fine and delicate.

clue.text: Stick up easy target

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, backwards

blocks.note: a mug is a gullible person, easily fooled

explanation.surface: A robber holding up a soft touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up' reads as a hold-up, but 'Stick' is the definition and 'up' the direction signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To gum things together is to glue them, making them adhere to each other.

clue.text: Front to shoe, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only final letters count

blocks.note: last letters of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Pointing out which end of the shoe is the front.
explanation.walkthrough: The ending letters of the three words spell the part they describe, so the whole clue is both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The toe of a shoe is its forward end, covering where the foot's digits sit.

clue.text: Concerning morning paper

blocks.note: re means regarding, as in a letter heading
a.m. stands for ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: Something to do with the morning newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paper' looks like a newspaper in the surface; it is stationery measured by quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: A ream is a standard pack of five hundred sheets of writing or printing stock.

clue.text: Retreat’s ghastly, not the last time

indicators.note: without its final piece, so the closing letter is dropped

blocks.note: hideous means horrible, ghastly
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A miserable retreat, though not the last time it will happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not the last time' looks like one phrase; it splits into the deletion signal and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideout is a secret refuge, somewhere to withdraw out of sight.
